translations.text: [?] He was a native of the region of Cappadocia. He had been a Christian since childhood, along with his parents.
Emperor Decius and the entire senate were at a loss because of the great crisis and helplessness that had arisen suddenly.
Emperor Decius ordered the military units and all the Roman regiments to assemble, so that they could go out to war and fight the barbarians.
For he was a man whose devotion to God was complete, and he lived with every kind of godliness.
The word of God was always sweeter in his mouth than honey.
One night, while he was sleeping among the troops, after he had finished praying, he dozed off for a little while.

Suddenly an angel of the Lord stood over him, touched his side, and woke him. The angel had a sword in his right hand. His appearance was frightening, and he wore a marvelous robe. When Saint Mercurius saw him, he was very afraid.
The angel addressed him, saying, “Mercurius!” He replied, “Here I am, my lord.”
Mercurius opened his eyes, and when he saw the angel, he was afraid, thinking that he was one of the emperor’s officials or a military commander.
When the emperor saw the bravery that Saint Mercurius had shown through the power of God, who was with him, he rejoiced greatly over the victory and the triumph that had come to the Romans.
His eyes were full of tears, and he wore a humble garment. They made him stand before the emperor.
“Now, then, tell me through whom this delusion came upon you.”
The blessed Mercurius answered, “As long as I have my Lord Jesus Christ helping him, I am not troubled by your tortures.”
“But [?] we do not know how he will die while he is alive, or how to make him stop. For the magic of the Christians is a hard wood that does not rot or decay.”
And he said, “I thank you, my Lord, because you have made me worthy to suffer for your holy name.”

A great miracle took place, worthy of being remembered. After the martyr had reached his end, his body became white like snow, giving off a sweet fragrance like choice incense. Because of this sign, many people became Christians.
“But if he disobeys us and our decree, he will be handed over to punishment by the sword, or to death by [?], or he will be given as food to the wild beasts and the birds.”
“Christians, especially, will be subject to a sentence of this kind.”
Changing their appearance, they too prepared their army to wage war against them. They ordered the regiments in every district and every city to come and assist them.

After they had continued in this way for many days, a man named Mercurius, who belonged to the regiment of those called the Martenses, saw a tall, radiant man wearing glorious clothes. He held a drawn sword in his right hand and said to him, “Mercurius, do not be afraid or be alarmed.”

His father was Gordian, who was the chief officer of this same regiment. The young man was approaching twenty-five years of age. For he had often heard his father say, “Blessed is the one who serves as a soldier under the King of heaven. He will grant him great, incomparable honors, and he will fight on his behalf against his enemies.”
For that King is the one who created everything by his word.

He established the sky like a vault and adorned it with shining stars, and the earth with beautiful, fragrant flowers to bring people comfort and healing. He also made the sea so that ships could sail on it, and made it a place where fish could be nourished.

And he is the one who is coming to judge the living and the dead and give each person according to their deeds. When Saint Mercurius recalled in his heart his father's words and the revelation he had seen, he became deeply troubled. He began to weep and sigh, saying, “Woe to him! I am the sinner, like a fruitless branch that has withered, having no root in the knowledge of God's glory.”
While he was still speaking, the emperor immediately sent two of those called silentiaries, together with some others, to summon him, because he was his adviser.
My father according to the flesh came from Scythia. His name was Gordian, and he served as a soldier in the regiment of the Martenses.

The emperor said to him, “Mercurius, what do you say? Will you obey our decree, which we have published for everyone, worship the gods, and receive your former honor and glory, or not? What do you say? Tell us quickly, since you know that you were brought here for this matter.”
A little later, at that very moment, the angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “Peace to you, victorious fighter!”
You have authority over my body, but God is the master of my soul.
At that time Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem, and a great sign of Christ appeared.
Basil said, “You have not read them properly, nor have you ever understood them. For if you had understood them, you would not despise them.”
He ordered Basil to be taken into the prison, together with the other two who were with him, and sent him to Persia.
They were not only eating, but also listening to the words of the wisdom that God had given him, as it is written: “Everything for the glory of God.”
When he had said these things, he went away, and I could no longer see him.
The clergy and the devoted workers sang psalms before him, with burning lamps, choice incense, and fragrant branches, until they brought him into the city.

After seven days, while all the people of the city were eating and drinking and celebrating with great joy because the saint's body had been revealed, the father of the little girl whose sight the saint had restored went to the bishop and asked for holy baptism.
When you rise early, come east to the city's first canal. You will find the little boy whom the mule injured because he wanted to strike you on account of my body.
And he will give you three gold coins, wishing to give them as a charitable offering.
He said to him with a laugh, “You did not take long to finish, brother!”
Immediately his hair came loose, fell out, and separated from his head, and he fell into a state of [?].

He too quickly established his brickworks near them, since he also wanted to build a courtyard in his house. One day he came and sat beside the laborers who were working. He got up and inspected the bricks until he came upon the saint's bricks, and he desired the saint's bricks more than all his own.
And if they say, ‘We will not let you take them away,’ I will beat them and carry them off by force, and see what this fellow called Mercurius will do to me.
After this, he called the poor man to whom Saint Mercurius had appeared. He said to him, “Come and tell me the quantity of my bricks and lime, because I want to build my house.”
Immediately, before the words had left his mouth, a camel standing in front of him opened its mouth, seized the pagan governor, threw him down beside it, and lay down on him.
When he had said these things, he hid himself from him.
And he was giving glory to the God of Saint Mercurius.

He said to him, “What are you doing here, you senseless man? This is not a place for grazing. You have let your horse come in. These trees and fruits belong to other people. And you came here to beat those working at my shrine. You did not work, nor did you let those who were working do their work.”
But they saw the man lying stretched out, unconscious. They did not know what had happened to him.
And a great crowd was coming to his holy relics and bowing down before them. The sick received healing and went back to their homes.

When a day had passed since the governor had come to the saint’s shrine, a governor of the city heard about his unmarried daughter, that she was very beautiful. He sent men from the city to him, saying, “I want to take your daughter as a wife for my son. I will increase her bride-price with gold and silver, male and female slaves, and ships that sail the sea, all in keeping with the honor of your greatness.”
The teacher would send the little boy every day, and he would tell the little girl what his teacher would write for him on his tablet.
And make the resting place. They engraved the martyr’s image inside it with colored stones [?], along with three gold crosses and three silver seals.
Immediately he cried out, “Help me, my beloved brother! While I was speaking with you, the saint slapped me in the face, and I have been terribly humiliated.”
And the governor himself also came and sat down.
